techniques.name: Algorithm Review Boards
techniques.description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

resources.title: How to design an AI ethics board
resources.abstract: The development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems poses significant risks to society. To reduce these risks to an acceptable level, AI companies need an effective risk management process and sound risk governance. In this paper, we explore a particular way in which AI companies can improve their risk governance: by setting up an AI ethics board. We identify five key design choices: (1) What responsibilities should the board have? (2) What should its legal structure be? (3) Who should sit on the board? (4) How should it make decisions? (5) And what resources does it need? We break each of these questions down into more specific sub-questions, list options, and discuss how different design choices affect the board’s ability to reduce societal risks from AI. Several failures have shown that designing an AI ethics board can be challenging. This paper provides a toolbox that can help AI companies to overcome these challenges.

resources.title: Designing Artificial Intelligence Review Boards: Creating Risk Metrics for Review of AI
resources.abstract: Discussions of the need for a review committee dedicated to ethical oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) research have not yet advanced to organization design discussions. What are the essential components for an AI research review board? Based upon precedent for composition and conduct of high-technology review boards, one essential component is a risk-adjusted review mechanism that assists review boards in the categorization of research needing review. In this paper, risk assessment tools are developed based upon lessons learned from other review boards, such as Institutional Biosafety Committees.

resources.title: Ethics and society review: Ethics reflection as a precondition to research funding
resources.abstract: Researchers in areas as diverse as computer science and political science must increasingly navigate the possible risks of their research to society. However, the history of medical experiments on vulnerable individuals influenced many research ethics reviews to focus exclusively on risks to human subjects rather than risks to human society. We describe an Ethics and Society Review board (ESR), which fills this moral gap by facilitating ethical and societal reflection as a requirement to access grant funding: Researchers cannot receive grant funding from participating programs until the researchers complete the ESR process for their proposal. Researchers author an initial statement describing their proposed research’s risks to society, subgroups within society, and globally and commit to mitigation strategies for these risks. An interdisciplinary faculty panel iterates with the researchers to refine these risks and mitigation strategies. We describe a mixed-method evaluation of the ESR over 1 y, in partnership with an artificial intelligence grant program run by Stanford HAI. Surveys and interviews of researchers who interacted with the ESR found 100% (95% CI: 87 to 100%) were willing to continue submitting future projects to the ESR, and 58% (95% CI: 37 to 77%) felt that it had influenced the design of their research project. The ESR panel most commonly identified issues of harms to minority groups, inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the research plan, dual use, and representation in datasets. These principles, paired with possible mitigation strategies, offer scaffolding for future research designs.

resources.title: ESR Process & Toolkit — Stanford Ethics & Society Review
resources.abstract: The Ethics and Society Review is improving ethical reflection in research by bringing together a panel of ethics experts to help researchers identify and mitigate negative ethical or societal aspects of their research and elevate the positive.

resources.title: Investigating Algorithm Review Boards for Organizational Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance
resources.abstract: Organizations are increasingly developing and utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Responsible AI (RAI) governance approaches including algorithm review board (ARBs) have emerged as important mechanisms to address potential AI risks and harms. We interviewed 17 technical contributors at a variety of organizations about their experiences with internal RAI governance. We summarized the first detailed findings on ARBs in practice, including their membership, scope, and measures of success. We confirmed known ARBs in finance sectors and revealed extensive use of ARBs in health sectors. Our findings suggest that Institutional Review Boards alone are insufficient for algorithm governance and that ARBs are used in tandem with other RAI approaches. Integration with existing processes and leadership buy-in were considered critical to the success of internal RAI governance. Financial tensions between profit and the cost of RAI were a major concern for many participants. Future work should explore measurements of success for ARBs and expand analysis of ARBs to other industries leading in AI implementation.

resources.title: A framework for the oversight and local deployment of safe and high-quality prediction models
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning models are being rapidly developed and used in clinical practice. However, many models are deployed without a clear understanding of clinical or operational impact and frequently lack monitoring plans that can detect potential safety signals. There is a lack of consensus in establishing governance to deploy, pilot, and monitor algorithms within operational healthcare delivery workflows. Here, we describe a governance framework that combines current regulatory best practices and lifecycle management of predictive models being used for clinical care. Since January 2021, we have successfully added models to our governance portfolio and are currently managing 52 models.

sample_claims.text: Every high-risk AI system was reviewed and approved by the organisation's algorithm review board before operational use, and the board could have blocked deployment
The conditions the review board attached to the credit-limit model's approval, including a disparate-impact analysis by protected group and a re-review date, were met before and after launch
The clinical decision-support model was deployed under a monitoring plan and re-review schedule set by a multidisciplinary review board independent of the development team
The diagnostic AI system's development and deployment decisions are traceable to dated board decision records that state the risks assessed, the reasons for approval and the conditions attached
The review board's decision record for the risk assessment tool, with its reasons and conditions, is available to the oversight body and the public

techniques.name: Red Teaming
techniques.description: Red teaming is a structured exercise in which a team deliberately tries to make an AI system fail, so that weaknesses are found before real users or attackers find them. The organisers set the scope and the harms of concern, recruit people with a mix of skills (for example security testers, domain specialists and members of affected groups), and give them a way to log each attempt and judge whether it worked. Participants try manipulative prompts, awkward edge cases and requests designed to draw out harmful, insecure or discriminatory responses, combining many approaches where a test for one known weakness, such as prompt injection, covers only one. The result is a record of the failures found and how easily each was provoked, which is not a pass or fail verdict. It feeds a risk register (the list of known risks and who owns them) and fixes, and the exercise is repeated when the system changes.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital convenes clinicians, medical students and engineers to stress-test a language model that drafts clinical notes, using real patient cases. Each response that could harm a patient, such as a wrong dosage, is logged and sent to the clinical safety officer to decide on fixes and on how staff may use the tool.

Before launch, a bank's security team and outside testers spend two weeks trying to make its customer-service assistant leak client data or obey instructions hidden in uploaded documents. Each successful attack is written up with the steps to reproduce it and ranked by how easily it was exploited, so engineers can fix the worst first.

A local authority asks advice charities and its own caseworkers to probe a chatbot that explains benefit entitlements. They look for answers that differ or discourage claims depending on a person's nationality, disability or first language, and record each case with the prompt that provoked it, for the authority to fix or justify.

An insurer's AI governance committee requires a red-team report before any customer-facing model goes live. Findings are entered in the risk register with an owner and a due date, and the committee signs off only when each high-severity item is fixed or formally accepted.

limitations.description: Needs people who understand both the system and how attackers work, and some harms need domain specialists to judge, for example whether chemical instructions are accurate. Exercises are therefore costly and hard to scale across many systems.

Finds only what the team thinks to try. In Anthropic's original exercise with 324 crowd workers, no attacks targeted code generation although the models had been trained partly on code, so coverage depends on who is recruited and how they are briefed.

Results describe one model version, configuration and set of safeguards at one moment. After an update or a prompt change, fixed failures can return and new ones appear, so the exercise has to be repeated, which adds cost each time.

Tester-written attacks may differ from real misuse, and there is no agreed measure of success. In Anthropic's study, participants' own ratings and an automated harm score correlated only imperfectly, and a minority of participants produced most attacks, so exercises are hard to compare.

A report with few findings can be read as proof of safety when it shows only that this team did not find a failure in the time available. Reports should state scope, effort and what was not tried, or they invite false confidence.

resources.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned
resources.abstract: We describe our early efforts to red team language models in order to simultaneously discover, measure, and attempt to reduce their potentially harmful outputs. We make three main contributions. First, we investigate scaling behaviors for red teaming across 3 model sizes (2.7B, 13B, and 52B parameters) and 4 model types: a plain language model (LM); an LM prompted to be helpful, honest, and harmless; an LM with rejection sampling; and a model trained to be helpful and harmless using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). We find that the RLHF models are increasingly difficult to red team as they scale, and we find a flat trend with scale for the other model types. Second, we release our dataset of 38,961 red team attacks for others to analyze and learn from. We provide our own analysis of the data and find a variety of harmful outputs, which range from offensive language to more subtly harmful non-violent unethical outputs. Third, we exhaustively describe our instructions, processes, statistical methodologies, and uncertainty about red teaming. We hope that this transparency accelerates our ability to work together as a community in order to develop shared norms, practices, and technical standards for how to red team language models.

resources.title: Red Teaming LLM Applications - DeepLearning.AI
Red teaming ChatGPT in medicine to yield real-world insights on model behavior
resources.abstract: Red teaming, the practice of adversarially exposing unexpected or undesired model behaviors, is critical towards improving equity and accuracy of large language models, but non-model creator-affiliated red teaming is scant in healthcare. We convened teams of clinicians, medical and engineering students, and technical professionals (80 participants total) to stress-test models with real-world clinical cases and categorize inappropriate responses along axes of safety, privacy, hallucinations/accuracy, and bias. Six medically-trained reviewers re-analyzed prompt-response pairs and added qualitative annotations. Of 376 unique prompts (1504 responses), 20.1% were inappropriate (GPT-3.5: 25.8%; GPT-4.0: 16%; GPT-4.0 with Internet: 17.8%). Subsequently, we show the utility of our benchmark by testing GPT-4o, a model released after our event (20.4% inappropriate). 21.5% of responses appropriate with GPT-3.5 were inappropriate in updated models. We share insights for constructing red teaming prompts, and present our benchmark for iterative model assessments.

sample_claims.text: A red-team exercise with clinicians and engineers tested the clinical-notes assistant against the hazards in its safety case, and every high-severity failure it found has a recorded fix or an accepted-risk decision.
The customer-service assistant was red-teamed for prompt injection and extraction of client data before launch, and each successful attack was fixed and re-tested.
A red-team exercise that included people from the affected groups probed the benefits assistant for discriminatory answers, and every case found has been triaged and fixed or formally accepted.
Each customer-facing model had a red-team report reviewed by the governance committee before release, and its open findings are logged in the risk register with owners and due dates.
Red-team attacks against the deployed assistant are repeated after every model or prompt change, and newly successful attacks are tracked until they are resolved.

techniques.name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
techniques.description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

A recruitment agency requires a named recruiter to confirm or reverse every automated rejection before it is sent, and logs the decision and the reason. The agency's governance board reviews the override rate each quarter to see whether the screening tool and its reviewers are working as intended.

limitations.description: Review capacity sets a ceiling. As volume rises, cases queue, decisions are delayed and time-sensitive uses become impractical, so the escalation rules must be tuned to what the available trained reviewers can handle.
Reviewers tire and drift. Attention and consistency fall over a long shift or a run of similar cases, so two reviewers, or one reviewer at different times, may decide the same case differently.

Automation bias. People tend to accept a system's recommendation, particularly under time pressure, so review can become a rubber stamp. A very high approval rate with almost no overrides may signal this rather than a good system.

The escalation rules decide what a human ever sees. A confidently wrong output passes without review when only low-confidence cases are escalated, so reviewing a random sample of routine cases is needed to find these errors.

Human review does not reliably improve decisions. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found human-AI combinations performed worse on average than the better of human or AI alone, with losses in decision-making tasks. The effect of a checkpoint should be tested, not assumed.

resources.title: Improving the Applicability of AI for Psychiatric Applications through Human-in-the-loop Methodologies
resources.abstract: Objectives Machine learning (ML) and natural language processing have great potential to improve efficiency and accuracy in diagnosis, treatment recommendations, predictive interventions, and scarce resource allocation within psychiatry. Researchers often conceptualize such an approach as operating in isolation without much need for human involvement, yet it remains crucial to harness human-in-the-loop practices when developing and implementing such techniques as their absence may be catastrophic. We advocate for building ML-based technologies that collaborate with experts within psychiatry in all stages of implementation and use to increase model performance while simultaneously increasing the practicality, robustness, and reliability of the process. Methods We showcase pitfalls of the traditional ML framework and explain how it can be improved with human-in-the-loop techniques. Specifically, we applied active learning strategies to the automatic scoring of a story recall task and compared the results to a traditional approach. Results Human-in-the-loop methodologies supplied a greater understanding of where the model was least confident or had knowledge gaps during training. As compared to the traditional framework, less than half of the training data were needed to reach a given accuracy. Conclusions Human-in-the-loop ML is an approach to data collection and model creation that harnesses active learning to select the most critical data needed to increase a model’s accuracy and generalizability more efficiently than classic random sampling would otherwise allow. Such techniques may additionally operate as safeguards from spurious predictions and can aid in decreasing disparities that artificial intelligence systems otherwise propagate.

resources.title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
resources.abstract: Technical developments in computer hardware and software now make it possible to introduce automation into virtually all aspects of human-machine systems. Given these technical capabilities, which system functions should be automated and to what extent? We outline a model for types and levels of automation that provides a framework and an objective basis for making such choices. Appropriate selection is important because automation does not merely supplant but changes human activity and can impose new coordination demands on the human operator. We propose that automation can be applied to four broad classes of functions: 1) information acquisition; 2) information analysis; 3) decision and action selection; and 4) action implementation. Within each of these types, automation can be applied across a continuum of levels from low to high, i.e., from fully manual to fully automatic. A particular system can involve automation of all four types at different levels. The human performance consequences of particular types and levels of automation constitute primary evaluative criteria for automation design using our model. Secondary evaluative criteria include automation reliability and the costs of decision/action consequences, among others. Examples of recommended types and levels of automation are provided to illustrate the application of the model to automation design.

resources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resources.abstract: Inspired by the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) to augment humans, researchers have studied human–AI systems involving different tasks, systems and populations. Despite such a large body of work, we lack a broad conceptual understanding of when combinations of humans and AI are better than either alone. Here we addressed this question by conducting a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of 106 experimental studies reporting 370 effect sizes. We searched an interdisciplinary set of databases (the Association for Computing Machinery Digital Library, the Web of Science and the Association for Information Systems eLibrary) for studies published between 1 January 2020 and 30 June 2023. Each study was required to include an original human-participants experiment that evaluated the performance of humans alone, AI alone and human–AI combinations. First, we found that, on average, human–AI combinations performed significantly worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges’ g = −0.23; 95% confidence interval, −0.39 to −0.07). Second, we found performance losses in tasks that involved making decisions and significantly greater gains in tasks that involved creating content. Finally, when humans outperformed AI alone, we found performance gains in the combination, but when AI outperformed humans alone, we found losses. Limitations of the evidence assessed here include possible publication bias and variations in the study designs analysed. Overall, these findings highlight the heterogeneity of the effects of human–AI collaboration and point to promising avenues for improving human–AI systems.

resources.title: Article 14: Human Oversight | EU Artificial Intelligence Act
Human-in-the-loop machine learning: a state of the art
resources.abstract: Researchers are defining new types of interactions between humans and machine learning algorithms generically called human-in-the-loop machine learning. Depending on who is in control of the learning process, we can identify: active learning, in which the system remains in control; interactive machine learning, in which there is a closer interaction between users and learning systems; and machine teaching, where human domain experts have control over the learning process. Aside from control, humans can also be involved in the learning process in other ways. In curriculum learning human domain experts try to impose some structure on the examples presented to improve the learning; in explainable AI the focus is on the ability of the model to explain to humans why a given solution was chosen. This collaboration between AI models and humans should not be limited only to the learning process; if we go further, we can see other terms that arise such as Usable and Useful AI. In this paper we review the state of the art of the techniques involved in the new forms of relationship between humans and ML algorithms. Our contribution is not merely listing the different approaches, but to provide definitions clarifying confusing, varied and sometimes contradictory terms; to elucidate and determine the boundaries between the different methods; and to correlate all the techniques searching for the connections and influences between them.

techniques.name: Confidence Thresholding
techniques.description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing tiered confidence thresholds in autonomous vehicle decision-making where high-confidence lane changes (>98%) execute automatically, medium-confidence decisions (85-98%) trigger additional sensor verification, and low-confidence situations (<85%) engage conservative defensive driving modes or request human takeover.

A diabetic eye-screening service has its image classifier pass the cases it is least sure about to an ophthalmologist. The service picks the referral share, for example the least certain 10 to 20 per cent of images, so that accuracy on the cases handled automatically meets its target.

A payment processor's fraud model approves transactions it scores as clearly legitimate, runs extra automated checks on middling scores, and sends the least certain ones to an analyst. The thresholds are set so that the analyst queue stays within the team's daily capacity.

A council's tool that flags possible errors in benefit claims shows caseworkers whether each flag is above or below its confidence threshold. The council publishes the share of claims sent to manual review and the error rate among those handled automatically, so the public can see when the tool declines to decide.

limitations.description: Many models produce poorly calibrated confidence scores that don't accurately reflect true prediction uncertainty, leading to overconfident predictions for incorrect outputs or underconfident scores for correct predictions.

Threshold selection requires careful calibration and domain expertise, as inappropriate thresholds can either overwhelm human reviewers with too many cases or miss genuinely uncertain decisions that need oversight.

High-confidence predictions may still be incorrect or harmful, particularly when models encounter adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution data, or systematic biases that the confidence mechanism doesn't detect.
Static thresholds may become inappropriate over time as model performance degrades, data distribution shifts occur, or operational contexts change, requiring ongoing monitoring and adjustment.
Withholding a prediction does not make the subsequent process safe. Review delays, failed routing and inadequate fallback capacity can undermine the intended safeguard.

resources.title: Improving speech recognition accuracy with multi-confidence thresholding
Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

sample_claims.text: The vehicle's planner switches to its conservative fallback whenever perception confidence falls below the validated threshold.

The deferral rate and the error rate among automatically handled cases at the operating threshold are documented and reported to the oversight board.

techniques.name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
techniques.description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's diagnostic-support service stops showing model suggestions to clinicians when the share of low-confidence predictions or the input drift score passes preset limits, for example after a scanner software update changes the images. A notice tells staff the standard workflow applies until engineers reset the breaker.

Deploying runtime monitoring for a recommendation engine that tracks recommendation diversity, click-through rates, and user engagement patterns, automatically switching to simpler algorithms when complex models show signs of performance degradation or unusual behaviour patterns.

A bank's credit-scoring service records every breaker state change, the metric that triggered it and the fallback used in an audit log. Model risk reviewers read the log each month to see how often, when and why the model was restricted, and whether the thresholds need revisiting.

An airline's customer-service assistant is wrapped in a circuit breaker that counts timeouts, blocked outputs and refusals. When they pass a limit after a faulty release, traffic switches to a scripted menu and the on-call engineer is paged, so the faulty version is stopped quickly without waiting for a manual decision.

limitations.description: Thresholds are hard to set. Too tight and the breaker trips on normal variation and withdraws a working service. Too loose and it stays closed through a real failure. Good settings need historical data from the live system, which is scarce at launch.

Model-level triggers are proxies for correctness. Drift scores and confidence can look normal while the model is confidently wrong, so a breaker that never trips is not evidence that predictions are right.

Gradual degradation and slow attacks can stay inside the limits, because each reading is acceptable while the cumulative effect is harmful. Catching them needs separate trend analysis or delayed accuracy checks alongside the breaker.

The breaker only moves the risk to the fallback. A cached answer, a simpler model or a human referral must itself be tested, and referral fails if reviewers cannot absorb a sudden diversion of traffic.

Tripping has a cost. A false trip withdraws a working service from users who may depend on it in time-critical settings, and reopening after a fixed cooldown, or on a few easy trial requests, can restore traffic before the underlying fault is fixed.

This paper argues it is dangerous to think ofthese quick wins as coming for free. Using the software engineering frameworkof technical debt, we find it is common to incur massive ongoing maintenancecosts in real-world ML systems. We explore several ML-specific risk factors toaccount for in system design. These include boundary erosion, entanglement,hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependencies, configurationissues, changes in the external world, and a variety of system-level anti-patterns.

resources.title: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor: A System for Real-Time Insights into Deployed Machine Learning Models
resources.abstract: With the increasing adoption of machine learning (ML) models and systems in high-stakes settings across different industries, guaranteeing a model's performance after deployment has become crucial. Monitoring models in production is a critical aspect of ensuring their continued performance and reliability. We present Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor, a fully managed service that continuously monitors the quality of machine learning models hosted on Amazon SageMaker. Our system automatically detects data, concept, bias, and feature attribution drift in models in real-time and provides alerts so that model owners can take corrective actions and thereby maintain high quality models. We describe the key requirements obtained from customers, system design and architecture, and methodology for detecting different types of drift. Further, we provide quantitative evaluations followed by use cases, insights, and lessons learned from more than two years of production deployment.

sample_claims.text: The diagnostic-support service stops showing model suggestions to clinicians when the share of low-confidence predictions or the input drift score passes its preset limit, and the standard clinical workflow applies until the breaker is reset.
The fraud-scoring service keeps answering requests during a model fault because the breaker diverts traffic to a rules-based fallback once the failure rate passes its threshold.
The forecasting service falls back to a simple baseline forecast when its inputs leave their historical ranges, so downstream users do not receive out-of-range forecasts.
Every breaker state change is recorded with its time, the metric that triggered it and the fallback used, and the log is available to system owners and auditors.
The platform records when its configured runtime restrictions activate and when normal calls resume.

techniques.name: Model Cards
techniques.description: A model card is a short structured document published with a trained model, stating what the model is for and what it should not be used for. It reports how the model performs on stated evaluation data, with results broken down by group (for example age or sex) and by operating condition (for example lighting or device) where these matter. It also records the training data, the metrics chosen and why, ethical considerations and known caveats. Readers use the card to judge whether the model suits their purpose before they deploy it. The original proposal gives suggested sections rather than a fixed format, and a card is only as reliable as the evaluation behind it.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical diagnosis AI with detailed performance metrics across different patient demographics, age groups, and clinical conditions, enabling healthcare providers to understand when the model should be trusted and when additional expert consultation is needed for patient safety.

Publishing a model card for a CV-screening model that reports selection rates and error rates for each gender and age band. An HR team deciding whether to adopt the tool can see where results differ between groups and ask the vendor for further evidence before using it.

Publishing detailed model documentation for a credit scoring API that clearly describes training data sources, evaluation methodologies, and performance limitations, enabling financial institutions to make informed decisions about model deployment and regulatory compliance.

A public body that buys AI tools asks each supplier for a model card and files it in its register of deployed models. Before approving a tool for a new use, officials compare the card's stated intended use and evaluation data with the proposed use and record any gaps.

limitations.description: Group-wise results need evaluation data labelled with the relevant attributes, which is often unavailable or restricted for privacy and legal reasons. Teams then report fewer groups than matter, and building the card takes time and statistical skill that can delay release.

Cards are written by the developer and nothing in the format requires an independent check. Unflattering results or commercially sensitive details can be left out, and a study of 32,111 Hugging Face model cards found the evaluation and limitations sections among the least often completed.

A card describes the model as evaluated at one point, on particular test data. Retraining, new deployment settings and data drift make it stale, and it stays in circulation unless someone owns updates and versioning.

A machine-readable model card format now exists (the model card object in the CycloneDX bill of materials, defined in ECMA-424, second edition, December 2025). The original template is still a set of suggested sections, and cards differ widely in structure and depth, which makes them hard to compare across models and vendors.

A card informs readers but does not constrain use or show that the model is safe. It cannot stop deployment outside the stated intended use, and the evidence it carries is only as good as the evaluations behind it.

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.abstract: Trained machine learning models are increasingly used to perform high-impact tasks in areas such as law enforcement, medicine, education, and employment. In order to clarify the intended use cases of machine learning models and minimize their usage in contexts for which they are not well suited, we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics. In this paper, we propose a framework that we call model cards, to encourage such transparent model reporting. Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions, such as across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups (e.g., race, geographic location, sex, Fitzpatrick skin type) and intersectional groups (e.g., age and race, or sex and Fitzpatrick skin type) that are relevant to the intended application domains. Model cards also disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, details of the performance evaluation procedures, and other relevant information. While we focus primarily on human-centered machine learning models in the application fields of computer vision and natural language processing, this framework can be used to document any trained machine learning model. To solidify the concept, we provide cards for two supervised models: One trained to detect smiling faces in images, and one trained to detect toxic comments in text. We propose model cards as a step towards the responsible democratization of machine learning and related AI technology, increasing transparency into how well AI technology works. We hope this work encourages those releasing trained machine learning models to accompany model releases with similar detailed evaluation numbers and other relevant documentation.

resources.title: Systematic analysis of 32,111 AI model cards characterizes documentation practice in AI
Interactive Model Cards: A Human-Centered Approach to Model Documentation
resources.abstract: Deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly adopted and deployed by analysts without formal training in NLP or machine learning (ML). However, the documentation intended to convey the model’s details and appropriate use is tailored primarily to individuals with ML or NLP expertise. To address this gap, we conduct a design inquiry into interactive model cards, which augment traditionally static model cards with affordances for exploring model documentation and interacting with the models themselves. Our investigation consists of an initial conceptual study with experts in ML, NLP, and AI Ethics, followed by a separate evaluative study with non-expert analysts who use ML models in their work. Using a semi-structured interview format coupled with a think-aloud protocol, we collected feedback from a total of 30 participants who engaged with different versions of standard and interactive model cards. Through a thematic analysis of the collected data, we identified several conceptual dimensions that summarize the strengths and limitations of standard and interactive model cards, including: stakeholders; design; guidance; understandability & interpretability; sensemaking & skepticism; and trust & safety. Our findings demonstrate the importance of carefully considered design and interactivity for orienting and supporting non-expert analysts using deep learning models, along with a need for consideration of broader sociotechnical contexts and organizational dynamics. We have also identified design elements, such as language, visual cues, and warnings, among others, that support interactivity and make non-interactive content accessible. We summarize our findings as design guidelines and discuss their implications for a human-centered approach towards AI/ML documentation.

sample_claims.text: The model's performance report identifies the assessed groups, operating conditions, metrics and evaluation datasets, including stated gaps.
The diagnostic model's card reports measured error differences and uncertainty for the specified patient groups and intersections.
The model's intended use cases and known limitations are clearly communicated to decision-makers
The lending model's card reports the selected group-comparison metrics and their assessment scope, without asserting equitable decisions from documentation alone.
The system's card records the stated training context, evaluation procedures and ethical considerations for inspection.

techniques.name: Datasheets for Datasets
techniques.description: A datasheet for a dataset is a short document that accompanies the dataset and answers a set of questions about it, in the way an electronic component comes with a datasheet. Gebru and colleagues group the questions into seven sections: why the dataset was made, what it contains, how it was collected, how it was cleaned and labelled, what it should and should not be used for, how it is distributed, and who maintains it. Creators read the questions before collecting data, answer them when the dataset is finished, and update the sheet when the dataset changes. People considering the dataset read it to judge whether it suits their task and what risks it carries. The questions are a prompt rather than a checklist, and a datasheet records what is known without testing it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model risk team asks a vendor for the datasheet of a transaction dataset before approving it for fraud-model training. The answers on how transactions were sampled, which merchants and periods are missing, and what the data should not be used for let the team judge whether the dataset fits its purpose.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

A hospital trust's data governance group will not release a medical imaging dataset to model developers until its datasheet is complete. The sheet records consent, anonymisation, sensitive attributes and sharing limits, and the group files it with the release approval as the record of what was checked.

A recruitment-technology team documents its CV dataset: the mix of applicants by job category and demographic group, how outcome labels were assigned, and which groups are thinly represented. Developers read this before training a screening model, so they know the limits of the data before they choose and test the model.

limitations.description: Writing a thorough datasheet takes time and knowledge of how the dataset was built, and the work recurs with each version, which can delay release. Gebru et al. note that the overhead is real and that organisational workflows and incentives need to change to accommodate it.

A datasheet describes the dataset as it was when written. Cleaning, augmentation or new data make it wrong unless it is revised, and Gebru et al. say the format fits dynamic datasets poorly, so each updated version needs an updated datasheet.

There is no single mandated template. Gebru et al. give a set of questions and say it is not prescriptive. ECMA-424 (CycloneDX 1.7, December 2025) standardises a machine-readable record of a dataset's contents, sensitive data and owners, but not the account of motivation, collection and intended use. Without enforcement, depth and completeness vary.

Answers come from the dataset's creators and nothing checks them. Creators may leave out sensitive details about collection, consent or bias to avoid legal or commercial exposure, so a datasheet can look complete and still mislead.

A datasheet records what its authors know. It does not measure bias, check coverage or find errors, and Gebru et al. note that spotting societal bias often needs demographic labels that creators may not hold. A clean-looking datasheet is not evidence the data suits a particular use.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.abstract: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains. To address this gap, we propose datasheets for datasets. In the electronics industry, every component, no matter how simple or complex, is accompanied with a datasheet that describes its operating characteristics, test results, recommended uses, and other information. By analogy, we propose that every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on. Datasheets for datasets will facilitate better communication between dataset creators and dataset consumers, and encourage the machine learning community to prioritize transparency and accountability.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning Practitioners' Data Documentation Perceptions, Needs, Challenges, and Desiderata
resources.abstract: Data is central to the development and evaluation of machine learning (ML) models. However, the use of problematic or inappropriate datasets can result in harms when the resulting models are deployed. To encourage responsible AI practice through more deliberate reflection on datasets and transparency around the processes by which they are created, researchers and practitioners have begun to advocate for increased data documentation and have proposed several data documentation frameworks. However, there is little research on whether these data documentation frameworks meet the needs of ML practitioners, who both create and consume datasets. To address this gap, we set out to understand ML practitioners' data documentation perceptions, needs, challenges, and desiderata, with the goal of deriving design requirements that can inform future data documentation frameworks. We conducted a series of semi-structured interviews with 14 ML practitioners at a single large, international technology company. We had them answer a list of questions taken from datasheets for datasets (Gebru, 2021). Our findings show that current approaches to data documentation are largely ad hoc and myopic in nature. Participants expressed needs for data documentation frameworks to be adaptable to their contexts, integrated into their existing tools and workflows, and automated wherever possible. Despite the fact that data documentation frameworks are often motivated from the perspective of responsible AI, participants did not make the connection between the questions that they were asked to answer and their responsible AI implications. In addition, participants often had difficulties prioritizing the needs of dataset consumers and providing information that someone unfamiliar with their datasets might need to know. Based on these findings, we derive seven design requirements for future data documentation frameworks.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets help ML Engineers Notice and Understand Ethical Issues in Training Data
resources.abstract: The social computing community has demonstrated interest in the ethical issues sometimes produced by machine learning (ML) models, like violations of privacy, fairness, and accountability. This paper discovers what kinds of ethical considerations machine learning engineers recognize, how they build understanding, and what decisions they make when working with a real-world dataset. In particular, it illustrates ways in which Datasheets for Datasets, an accountability intervention designed to help engineers explore unfamiliar training data, scaffolds the process of issue discovery, understanding, and ethical decision-making. Participants were asked to review an intentionally ethically problematic dataset and asked to think aloud as they used it to solve a given ML problem. Out of 23 participants, 11 were given a Datasheet they could use while completing the task. Participants were ethically sensitive enough to identify concerns in the dataset; participants who had a Datasheet did open and refer to it; and those with Datasheets mentioned ethical issues during the think-aloud earlier and more often than than those without. The think-aloud protocol offered a grounded description of how participants recognized, understood, and made a decision about ethical problems in an unfamiliar dataset. The method used in this study can test other interventions that claim to encourage recognition, promote understanding, and support decision-making among technologists.

The dataset's composition by demographic group and its sampling method are documented, so model developers can judge whether the data represents the population the model will serve.

techniques.name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
techniques.description: MLflow is an open-source platform that tracks machine learning experiments by automatically logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts throughout the ML lifecycle. It provides a centralised repository for comparing different experimental runs, reproducing results, and managing model versions. Teams can track hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, model files, and execution environment details, creating a comprehensive audit trail that supports collaboration, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance across the entire machine learning development process.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical diagnosis model experiments across different hospitals, logging hyperparameters, performance metrics, and model artifacts to ensure reproducible research and enable regulatory audits of model development processes.

Managing fraud detection model versions in production, tracking which specific model configuration and training data version is deployed, enabling quick rollback and performance comparison when system reliability issues arise.

Documenting loan approval model experiments with complete parameter tracking and performance logging across demographic groups, supporting fair lending compliance by providing transparent records of model development and validation processes.

limitations.description: Requires teams to adopt disciplined logging practices and may introduce overhead to development workflows if not properly integrated into existing processes.
Storage costs can grow substantially with extensive artifact logging, especially for large models or high-frequency experimentation.
Tracking quality depends on developers consistently logging relevant information, with incomplete logging leading to gaps in experimental records.
Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively.
Security and access control configurations require careful setup to protect sensitive model information and experimental data in shared environments.

resources.title: Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow
resources.abstract: Machine learning development creates multiple new challenges that are not present in a traditional software development lifecycle. These include keeping track of the myriad inputs to an ML application (e.g., data versions, code and tuning parameters), reproducing results, and production deployment. In this paper, we summarize these challenges from our experience with Databricks customers, and describe MLflow, an open source platform we recently launched to streamline the machine learning lifecycle. MLflow covers three key challenges: experimentation, reproducibility, and model deployment, using generic APIs that work with any ML library, algorithm and programming language. The project has a rapidly growing open source community, with over 50 contributors since its launch in June 2018.

An MLOps Framework for Explainable Network Intrusion Detection with MLflow
resources.abstract: The surge in network traffic has required advanced techniques to ensure network security. Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs), which increasingly employ Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methodologies, play a pivotal role in this task by continuously monitoring network traffic patterns and identifying suspicious activities. To address the complexities of developing ML- and DL-based NIDS, MLOps tools have been designed to optimize model deployment, monitoring, and management in production environments, streamlining model development. These tools enable efficient experimentation, version management, and logging of artifacts for network administrators and data scientists. In this work, we design a framework powered by MLflow to manage the ML pipeline from data handling to results visualization. To show the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted an experimental campaign on 4 broadly used security datasets (viz. NSL-KDD, IoT-23, Kitsune, and TON_IoT) performing crucial tasks for intrusion detection, namely anomaly detection, binary misuse detection, and multiclass misuse detection.

resources.title: Enhancing Quantum Software Development Process with Experiment Tracking
resources.abstract: As quantum computing advances from theoretical promise to experimental reality, the need for rigorous experiment tracking becomes critical. Drawing inspiration from best practices in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), we argue that reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration in quantum research can benefit significantly from structured tracking workflows. This paper explores the application of MLflow in quantum research, illustrating how it enables better development practices, experiment reproducibility, decision making, and cross-domain integration in an increasingly hybrid classical-quantum landscape.

techniques.name: Data Version Control
techniques.description: Data Version Control (DVC) is a Git-like version control system specifically designed for machine learning data, models, and experiments. It tracks changes to large data files, maintains reproducible ML pipelines, and creates a complete audit trail of data transformations, model training, and evaluation processes. DVC works alongside Git to provide end-to-end lineage tracking from raw data through preprocessing, training, and deployment, enabling teams to reproduce any model version and understand exactly how datasets evolved throughout the ML lifecycle.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical imaging dataset versions and model training pipelines to ensure reproducible research results, enabling hospitals to verify which specific data version and preprocessing steps were used for regulatory submissions.

Managing credit scoring model data pipelines with complete version control of training datasets, feature engineering steps, and model artifacts, ensuring reliable model reproduction and rollback capabilities when performance issues arise.

Maintaining pharmaceutical drug discovery data lineage across multiple research teams, tracking compound datasets, feature extraction processes, and model versions to support FDA submissions with complete experimental provenance.

limitations.description: Requires learning Git-like workflows and CLI commands, which may have a steep learning curve for teams unfamiliar with version control systems.
Storage costs can be substantial for large datasets with frequent changes, especially when maintaining multiple versions and branches of data.
Complex data pipelines with many interdependencies may require significant setup time and careful configuration to track properly.
Performance can degrade with very large files or datasets due to checksumming and synchronisation overhead during operations.
Team coordination becomes essential as improper branch management or merge conflicts can disrupt collaborative workflows.

resources.title: Get Started with DVC
On the Co-evolution of ML Pipelines and Source Code - Empirical Study of DVC Projects
resources.abstract: The growing popularity of machine learning (ML) applications has led to the introduction of software engineering tools such as Data Versioning Control (DVC), MLFlow and Pachyderm that enable versioning ML data, models, pipelines and model evaluation metrics. Since these versioned ML artifacts need to be synchronized not only with each other, but also with the source and test code of the software applications into which the models are integrated, prior findings on co-evolution and coupling between software artifacts might need to be revisited. Hence, in order to understand the degree of coupling between ML-related and other software artifacts, as well as the adoption of ML versioning features, this paper empirically studies the usage of DVC in 391 Github projects, 25 of which in detail. Our results show that more than half of the DVC files in a project are changed at least once every one-tenth of the project's lifetime. Furthermore, we observe a tight coupling between DVC files and other artifacts, with 1/4 pull requests changing source code and 1/2 pull requests changing tests requiring a change to DVC files. As additional evidence of the observed complexity associated with adopting ML-related software engineering tools like DVC, an average of 78% of the studied projects showed a non-constant trend in pipeline complexity.

resources.title: DVC in Open Source ML-development: The Action and the Reaction
resources.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) systems are gaining popularity, reshaping various domains ranging from customer services to software engineering. The effectiveness of ML systems is dependent on the quality of their training data. Therefore, practitioners invest substantial time experimenting with different data, parameters, and models to guarantee the quality of the end system. Prior work highlighted unique challenges of developing ML systems, particularly concerning versioning data and models. Recently, various tools such as DVC and MLFlow have emerged to aid developers in the storage and tracking of data. Despite their growing popularity, very little is known about their usage patterns and impact on open-source software (OSS) systems. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study on 56 GitHub OSS projects that use DVC to understand the DVC usage pattern and the impact of using DVC on the software development process. We found that Versioning and tracking is the most adopted DVC feature, being utilized by all 56 projects and being the only adopted feature in 85.7% of them. Furthermore, we found that DVC has a significant impact on the software development process indicators such as the number of created pull requests (PRs), and the number of bug-fix commits. For instance, our findings showed that DVC causes a peak in the number of commits and PRs at the moment of the adoption, followed by a long-term decrease. We believe that our findings can assist practitioners in tailoring tools to better meet user requirements and help organizations realize potential outcomes of adopting such tools.

The model's performance can be recreated using the exact dataset version and pipeline configuration from any prior release

techniques.name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
techniques.description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

example_use_cases.description: A fraud-scoring API provider examines each client's query stream for runs of near-identical transactions altered in small steps, which suggest someone is probing for the score at which a transaction passes. Flagged accounts are rate-limited and sent to the security team for review.

A company selling traffic-sign recognition as a paid API tests whether the spacing between each customer's successive image queries follows the pattern ordinary use produces. Accounts whose queries look synthetic and widely spread, as in model-copying attacks, are flagged for investigation and possible suspension.

A health-technology company serving a paediatric triage model to many clinics monitors each clinic's query volumes and the ages in its requests. A clinic sending mostly adult patients, or a sudden change after a software update, is flagged so the company can contact it before unsafe advice is given.

A provider of a text-generation API scores each customer's usage by how often prompts and responses are flagged as harmful and whether jailbreak attempts recur. Customers with high scores go to review, which can lead to a warning or suspension.

A bank's model risk team compares the monthly log of calls to its credit-scoring API, by internal team and purpose, with the uses approved at validation. The comparison is filed in the model's audit record, so reviewers can see whether the model is used as documented.

limitations.description: Anomalies are defined against a baseline of normal use, and ordinary users can be unusual. In PRADA's tests, legitimate queries made of consecutive frames from a sequence triggered false alarms at stricter settings, so the alert threshold has to be tuned to each model and use case.

A patient attacker can stay inside normal limits by querying slowly, adding dummy queries or spreading queries across many accounts. PRADA's authors show that padding queries raises the attacker's cost three to ten times, and that multiple accounts defeat per-account analysis.

Useful monitoring needs request content, or features of it, to be logged and sometimes read by reviewers. For sensitive applications that may be unlawful or unacceptable, and Microsoft notes that detection may be less accurate when human review is switched off for such customers.

Detectors keep state for every account. PRADA's authors estimate a few gigabytes in total for a few hundred clients of an image model, and the cost rises with traffic and with the retention period set for audit evidence.

The published extraction detectors were tested on small models, decision trees in one case and image classifiers in the other, against simulated attackers. Kesarwani et al. describe their warning as approximate, so an alert is a lead for investigation, not proof of theft.

resources.title: Model Extraction Warning in MLaaS Paradigm
resources.abstract: Machine learning models deployed on the cloud are susceptible to several security threats including extraction attacks. Adversaries may abuse a model's prediction API to steal the model thus compromising model confidentiality, privacy of training data, and revenue from future query payments. This work introduces a model extraction monitor that quantifies the extraction status of models by continually observing the API query and response streams of users. We present two novel strategies that measure either the information gain or the coverage of the feature space spanned by user queries to estimate the learning rate of individual and colluding adversaries. Both approaches have low computational overhead and can easily be offered as services to model owners to warn them against state of the art extraction attacks. We demonstrate empirical performance results of these approaches for decision tree and neural network models using open source datasets and BigML MLaaS platform.

resources.title: PRADA: Protecting Against DNN Model Stealing Attacks
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) applications are increasingly prevalent. Protecting the confidentiality of ML models becomes paramount for two reasons: (a) a model can be a business advantage to its owner, and (b) an adversary may use a stolen model to find transferable adversarial examples that can evade classification by the original model. Access to the model can be restricted to be only via well-defined prediction APIs. Nevertheless, prediction APIs still provide enough information to allow an adversary to mount model extraction attacks by sending repeated queries via the prediction API. In this paper, we describe new model extraction attacks using novel approaches for generating synthetic queries, and optimizing training hyperparameters. Our attacks outperform state-of-the-art model extraction in terms of transferability of both targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples (up to +29-44 percentage points, pp), and prediction accuracy (up to +46 pp) on two datasets. We provide take-aways on how to perform effective model extraction attacks. We then propose PRADA, the first step towards generic and effective detection of DNN model extraction attacks. It analyzes the distribution of consecutive API queries and raises an alarm when this distribution deviates from benign behavior. We show that PRADA can detect all prior model extraction attacks with no false positives.

techniques.name: Data Poisoning Detection
techniques.description: Data poisoning detection looks for training examples that an attacker has planted to change how a model behaves. The best-studied case is the backdoor: a few examples carrying a hidden trigger, such as a sticker on a stop sign, are mislabelled so that the model misclassifies any input with the trigger while it performs normally on clean data. Detection first trains a model on the untrusted data, then examines how that model represents each training example internally (its activations in the last hidden layer), one class at a time. Activation clustering splits a class into two groups by those activations and flags the smaller group when the split is clear, and spectral signatures score each example by its position along the main direction of variation and flag the highest scores. The flagged examples are reviewed or removed and the model is retrained, which yields a list of suspected examples and a measure of how cleanly each class separates.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a traffic-sign classifier for a driver-assistance system trains a trial model on images gathered from several suppliers and runs activation clustering on each class. A small separate group of stop-sign images labelled as speed limits, all carrying the same sticker, is flagged and removed before the final training run.

A research platform builds a chest X-ray classifier from images contributed by many partner hospitals. Before any partner's images enter the training set, it trains a trial model and scores each class for the small, separable group of examples a planted backdoor leaves, because one contributor's data could be compromised.

A platform trains a harmful-content classifier on labels supplied by crowd workers. Analysts scan each class for a small separate group of examples sharing a trigger phrase and labelled as harmless, which would let that phrase slip past the filter, and remove them before retraining.

An insurer trains a damage-assessment classifier on claims photos labelled by an outside vendor. Before relying on the labels, it scores each class for a small, separate group of photos carrying the same mark and labelled undamaged, which a compromised vendor account could have planted so that damaged vehicles with the mark pass unchecked. Flagged photos go back to the vendor for explanation.

limitations.description: An attacker who knows the detector can adapt. Both methods rely on poisoned examples standing out in the model's learned representation, so an attack that keeps them close to genuine examples can slip through. Chen et al. found no obvious way round activation clustering within their threat model, but say further work is needed.

False alarms can remove legitimate but unusual examples, reducing data quality and diversity. Chen et al. suggest a silhouette-score cut-off of about 0.10 to 0.15 based on three datasets; another data type or model may need different values, and a wrong value either removes good data or leaves poison in.

Both methods assume poisoned examples are a minority that separates from clean ones in the learned representation, and Tran et al.'s needs an upper bound on how many there are. They were designed and tested on backdoors in image and text classifiers, so attacks that only lower overall accuracy lie outside what the original papers show.

Both methods first train a model on the untrusted data, read its internal activations, then retrain after removing flagged examples. They need the full training data and white-box access to the model, and cost at least two training runs, so they cannot be applied to a model someone else trained when the data or weights are unavailable.

Real poison is unlabelled, so a detector's accuracy can only be measured on poison the tester injects, and a clean result shows that this detector found nothing, not that the data is clean. Telling poison from naturally unusual data is hard.

resources.title: Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by Activation Clustering
resources.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models are being increasingly trusted to make decisions in different and varying areas, the safety of systems using such models has become an increasing concern. In particular, ML models are often trained on data from potentially untrustworthy sources, providing adversaries with the opportunity to manipulate them by inserting carefully crafted samples into the training set. Recent work has shown that this type of attack, called a poisoning attack, allows adversaries to insert backdoors or trojans into the model, enabling malicious behavior with simple external backdoor triggers at inference time and only a blackbox perspective of the model itself. Detecting this type of attack is challenging because the unexpected behavior occurs only when a backdoor trigger, which is known only to the adversary, is present. Model users, either direct users of training data or users of pre-trained model from a catalog, may not guarantee the safe operation of their ML-based system. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to backdoor detection and removal for neural networks. Through extensive experimental results, we demonstrate its effectiveness for neural networks classifying text and images. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first methodology capable of detecting poisonous data crafted to insert backdoors and repairing the model that does not require a verified and trusted dataset.

resources.title: Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks
resources.abstract: A recent line of work has uncovered a new form of data poisoning: so-called \emph{backdoor} attacks. These attacks are particularly dangerous because they do not affect a network's behavior on typical, benign data. Rather, the network only deviates from its expected output when triggered by a perturbation planted by an adversary. In this paper, we identify a new property of all known backdoor attacks, which we call \emph{spectral signatures}. This property allows us to utilize tools from robust statistics to thwart the attacks. We demonstrate the efficacy of these signatures in detecting and removing poisoned examples on real image sets and state of the art neural network architectures. We believe that understanding spectral signatures is a crucial first step towards designing ML systems secure against such backdoor attacks
